extracted.intended_audience: patent litigators, patent prosecutors, and courts deciding 35 U.S.C. § 101 eligibility
extracted.subtask_description: Legal standards and factual-evidence rules for evaluating patent eligibility under the Alice two-step framework on a Rule 12(b)(6) motion, with application to network/software claims. Focuses on when a claim can be dismissed as abstract and what counts as an 'inventive concept.'

rubrics_metrics.name: Alice two-step framework
rubrics_metrics.description: Apply the Supreme Court’s two-step Alice framework: (1) determine whether the claim is "directed to" a "patent-ineligible concept," such as an abstract idea; (2) if so, examine the claim elements to determine whether they contain an "inventive concept" sufficient to "transform" the claimed abstract idea into a patent-eligible application.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Use Alice Corp. v. CLS Bank Int’l, 573 U.S. 208, 217, 221 (2014) as governing authority. If step one finds the claim directed to an abstract idea, proceed to step two to assess presence of an inventive concept (quoting Mayo as necessary).

rubrics_metrics.name: Inventive concept standard
rubrics_metrics.description: An "inventive concept" is more than merely implementing an abstract idea using "well-understood, routine, [and] conventional activities previously known to the industry."
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Assess whether claim elements, individually and as an ordered combination, provide something beyond conventional computer implementation (see Content Extraction & Transmission LLC v. Wells Fargo Bank, Nat’l Ass’n, 776 F.3d 1343, 1347–48).

rubrics_metrics.name: When eligibility may be resolved on Rule 12(b)(6)
rubrics_metrics.description: Patent eligibility may be resolved at the Rule 12 stage only if there are no plausible factual disputes after drawing all reasonable inferences from the intrinsic and Rule 12 record in favor of the non-movant.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Cite and follow precedent (e.g., Visual Memory v. NVIDIA; CardioNet v. InfoBionic; Aatrix; Berkheimer). If plausible factual disputes exist about inventiveness or conventionality, dismissal is improper.

rubrics_metrics.name: Conventionality is a factual inquiry (Berkheimer rule)
rubrics_metrics.description: Whether claim elements are "well-understood, routine, or conventional" is often a question of fact; a material dispute of fact over conventionality precludes dismissal or summary adjudication on §101.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: District courts should not resolve such disputes against the non-movant at the 12(b)(6) stage; evidentiary development may be required (see Berkheimer v. HP, Inc., 881 F.3d 1360).

rubrics_metrics.name: Adopt non-moving party’s claim construction on motion to dismiss where appropriate
rubrics_metrics.description: When claim scope is disputed on a Rule 12 motion and the district court has not conducted claim construction, the court should proceed by adopting the non-moving party’s construction for purposes of the motion.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Follow Aatrix Software, Inc. v. Green Shades Software, Inc., 882 F.3d 1121, 1125; do not resolve disputed claim-meaning questions against the patentee on 12(b)(6).

rubrics_metrics.name: Specific structural/functional claim limitations can supply inventive concept
rubrics_metrics.description: Claims that recite a specific technical solution—i.e., particular arrangements of elements, network structure, or functional limitations that improve computer/network functioning—can constitute an inventive concept sufficient to survive §101 challenge.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Look for claim language that delineates structure and function and for specification statements tying those features to improved performance (see BASCOM; Enfish; Thales; SRI). Courts should consider whether the claimed arrangement is a technical improvement over prior art ways of arranging systems.

rubrics_metrics.name: Specification and pleading allegations can create plausible factual issues
rubrics_metrics.description: Statements in the patent specification, prosecution history, and well-pleaded allegations in the complaint can plausibly allege inventive concepts and improvements, creating factual disputes that preclude dismissal.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: At the 12(b)(6) stage draw all inferences in favor of the patentee and weigh specification/prosecution statements when determining plausibility (citing Cellspin, Berkheimer, Aatrix).

rubrics_metrics.name: Absence of external supporting evidence is not always fatal on Rule 12
rubrics_metrics.description: Although supporting evidence (e.g., expert declarations or prior art citations) can strengthen inventive-concept allegations, the lack of such evidence in the complaint does not automatically require dismissal at the pleading stage.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: District courts may still deny dismissal where the complaint and patent specification plausibly allege inventive features (see Nat. Alternatives).

rubrics_metrics.name: Patentability of improvements using conventional components
rubrics_metrics.description: Useful improvements to computer networks or systems are patentable even if realized with standard computing equipment; novelty can lie in architecture/arrangement rather than exotic hardware.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Do not conflate use of conventional components with absence of inventive concept; evaluate whether the claimed combination or arrangement yields a technical improvement (Thales Visionix; Enfish).

rubrics_metrics.name: Plausible factual allegations tethered to claim limitations defeat dismissal
rubrics_metrics.description: If the complaint plausibly alleges that specific claimed limitations provided new or improved functionality (e.g., reduced cost, improved redundancy, smoother playback), those allegations tethered to claim language create a factual dispute precluding 12(b)(6) dismissal.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Assess whether alleged benefits are tied to the claim elements (e.g., capacity improvements tied to distribution outside CDN). If so, treat as plausible inventive-concept allegations (see Berkheimer and the opinion's application).

rubrics_metrics.name: Dynamic P2P network structural limitation (as an alleged inventive concept)
rubrics_metrics.description: Claim must include at least one P2P dynamic network with a multiplicity of peer nodes that "consume the same content within a predetermined time" and are "distributed outside controlled networks and/or content distribution networks (CDNs)."
rubrics_metrics.guidance: This structural limitation is alleged to be inventive because it (per the specification) groups peers by simultaneous content consumption to provide smooth playback, avoid stuttering/buffering, improve redundancy, address capacity problems, and reduce CDN costs; courts should treat such structural-functional recitations as potential inventive concepts.

rubrics_metrics.name: Content segmentation based on trace routes (as an alleged inventive concept)
rubrics_metrics.description: Claim requires content segmentation "based on CDN address resolution, trace route to CDN and P2P server manager, dynamic feedback from peers reporting traffic rates between individual peer and its neighbors, round-robin and other server side scheduling/resource allocation techniques."
rubrics_metrics.guidance: The specification and prosecution history describe segmenting using trace routes as a factor for balancing/managing distribution and improving reliability, redundancy, and efficiency. If the claim requires trace-route-based segmentation (and the complaint pleads it does), that limitation can be an inventive concept; courts should not assume trace-route usage is merely conventional without resolving factual disputes.
